A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GraphArena and provide readable main text, figures, tables, task definitions, and appendices. Retained, revised, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs on 10,000 graph problems, including benchmark scores, graph-size and prompting analyses, and comparisons with TSP solvers.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and additional experiments involving fine-tuning, code execution, test-time compute, GNNs, graph encodings, and synthetic graphs.

M1.justification: Although the core GraphArena construction and scoring framework remain stable, v2 Section 3.2 adds substantial solving procedures: supervised fine-tuning on GraphArena solution paths, generated-code execution, checker-selected parallel sampling, and sequential checker-guided hinting. v1 tested CoT and an existing GraphWiz checkpoint, while code solving was future work. The expanded description of the existing checker alone does not establish a scorer change.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix C and Table 8 add evaluation on synthetic Erdos-Renyi graphs for Common Neighbor and Shortest Distance. The five real-world graph sources and ten original tasks remain. The additional fine-tuning examples increase sample coverage within these tasks rather than introducing a new task domain.

E2.justification: The main comparison replaces GPT-3.5, Claude-haiku, and the Qwen1.5 models with GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-sonnet, GLM-4-plus, and Qwen2.5-72b. v2 additionally evaluates GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE, and GraphToken, retains GraphWiz, and adds classical solver comparisons for GED, MIS, and MVC beyond the original TSP comparison. The CoT comparison also replaces Llama3-70b with Llama3-8b and drops Claude-haiku.

E3.justification: v2 introduces training on 10,000 additional supervised problems, GNN evaluation using numerical answers rather than solution paths, and compute-scaling experiments with up to 16 parallel or five sequential attempts. GPT-4o changes from the May 2024 snapshot to the August 2024 snapshot. The original benchmark's task-specific graph-size ranges, 500 small and 500 large instances per task, and temperature 0.1 remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained graph-size and CoT analyses, v2 tests graph-encoding sensitivity and real-versus-synthetic graph difficulty in Tables 7–8. Tables 2–3 and Figure 7 examine the benefits and limitations of fine-tuning, code execution, and additional inference attempts. Figure 5 adds a GraphToken comparison with its GNN and LLM backbones.

E5.justification: Both versions explicitly report a single benchmark run per model and provide no confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based uncertainty estimates. The new multiple-attempt inference experiments study compute scaling rather than statistical uncertainty across experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises scores and rankings, with Claude-3.5-sonnet replacing GPT-4o as the reported leading model. Even retained model entries change beyond rounding: Llama3-70b's large-NP feasibility changes from 48.77% to 45.0%. v2 adds extensive mitigation, GNN, encoding, synthetic-graph, and non-TSP solver results. Updated GPT-4o scores use a different stated snapshot and therefore do not establish a controlled same-model improvement.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definitions and feasibility/optimality requirements are retained, including the five NP-task definitions moved to Appendix B. Neither version develops formal proofs or derivations. The new reasoning terminology and discussion of previously published GNN expressiveness results do not introduce new formal theory.

C1.justification: v2 broadens the central contribution from benchmarking limitations to experimentally exploring four routes for improving graph computation. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion add claims about the benefits and limits of instruction tuning, code execution, and test-time compute. Task selection is also reframed around direct algorithmic reasoning versus meta algorithmic planning, replacing the earlier System 1/System 2 framing.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning synthetic benchmarks potentially overstating generalization, graph encoding effects, limited benefits of fine-tuning and compute scaling, and code-generation or graph-extraction failures. It discusses the different GNN evaluation paradigm and limitations of graph–LLM integration. GraphWiz's poor transfer is attributed to task and graph-format mismatch rather than the earlier additional speculation about reliance on pattern recognition.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents full-parameter tuning with learning rate 0.0001, cosine scheduling, warmup ratio 0.1, and batch size 4. It also specifies regular-expression answer extraction and exact-solver ground truth. These are useful but limited disclosures; the hardware, repository link, and original prompt examples remain, while relocated dataset descriptions and licenses are not new information.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive Neural Algorithmic Reasoning discussion and positions GraphArena relative to CLRS, CLRS-Text, MAGMA, and learned combinatorial optimization. New references support tool-based reasoning, inference scaling, GNN comparisons, and additional approximation algorithms, while portions of the broader LLM-evaluation survey are removed. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, evaluation explanation, experimental narrative, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are organized around evaluation and enhancement questions. Dataset descriptions and five task definitions move into separate appendices, and the original appendix becomes a three-part organization. The title, author list, and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds solver-comparison bars, GraphToken plots, compute-scaling curves, and five experimental tables. The original TSP table becomes a wider four-task appendix table, and dataset statistics gain density and edge-connectivity columns. Existing radar, hallucination, and CoT plots are revised and rearranged within the new conference layout; the original prompt tables are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 provides useful evidence for previously asserted benchmark-design choices and explores practical mitigation strategies beyond v1's limited CoT and GraphWiz tests. However, new reporting problems weaken these gains: Table 2 gives Llama3-8b large-polynomial accuracy as 20.2%, versus 9.4% in Table 1, and the DeepSeek code experiment leaves model changes versus prompting effects unclear. The broader diagnostic evidence improves the paper, but these consistency and attribution issues limit the net quality gain.
